provenance.notes: Low-acid foods (vegetables, meat, fish) must be pressure canned. Water bath canning is limited to high-acid foods. Failure to follow verified processing times carries lethal botulism risks.

methods.name: Water Bath Canning
methods.equipment: Large stockpot, jar lifter, canning jars/lids

methods.name: Pressure Canning
methods.foods: Low-acid foods (Vegetables, meat, poultry, fish, soups)
methods.equipment: Dial/Weighted Gauge Pressure Canner, canning accessories
methods.risk: High (canner failure or under-processing allows botulism survival)

methods.name: Dehydrating

methods.name: Root Cellaring
methods.foods: Potatoes, carrots, onions, garlic, apples, winter squash
methods.equipment: Ventilated boxes, damp sand (for root crops), dark cool room

safetyFlow.desc: Identify food pH. If pH is above 4.6 (e.g., green beans, carrots, beef), you MUST use a pressure canner. Boiling water bath is NOT safe for low-acid foods.
Check jars for cracks, nicks, or chips along the rim. Rims must be completely smooth to achieve a vacuum hermetic seal.
Wash jars. Fill with food, leaving the exact headspace specified by the recipe (typically 1/2" for fruit/pickles, 1" for meats/vegetables).
Wipe jar rims with a clean damp cloth to remove any grease or residue. Center clean lid on jar, and screw band down to fingertip-tight.
Process in canner according to altitude-adjusted times. Let jars cool undisturbed for 12-24 hours. Check seals (lids should not flex when pressed).

rootCellarRules.rule: Maintain 32°F to 40°F. Temperatures above 45°F speed rot and trigger sprouting.
Aim for 85-95% relative humidity for roots (carrots, potatoes) to prevent shriveling. Store in damp sand.
Never store apples/pears near potatoes. Apples release ethylene gas which causes potatoes to sprout and rot.

timeline.title: Root Crops & Meats
